div.head: SUBSECT. 4.
Philtres, Magical, and Poetical cures.
div.p:
Where persuasions and other remedies will not take place, many fly to unlawful means, Philtres, Amulets, Magic spells, Ligatures, Characters, Charms, which as a wound with the spear of Achilles, if so made and caused, must so be cured. If forced by Spells and Philtres, saith Paracelsus, it must be eased by Characters, Mag. lib. 2 cap. 28, and by Incantations. Fernelius Path. lib. 6 cap. 13, Extinguitur virilitas ex incantamentorum maleficiis, neque enim fabula est, nonnulli reperti sunt qui ex veneficiis amore privati sunt, ut ex multis historiis patet [Virility is extinguished by the sorcery of incantations. Indeed, this no fable: several can be found who have been stripped of love by magical means, as is evident from many accounts].Schenkius lib. 4 observ. Med. hath some examples of such as have been so magically caused, and magically cured, and by witchcraft: so saith Baptista Codronchus, lib. 3 cap. 6 de morb. ven., Malleus malef. cap. 6. ’Tis not permitted to be done, I confess: yet often attempted: see more in Wierus lib. 3 cap. 18 de praestig. de remediis per Philtra, Delrio Tom. 2 lib. 3 quaest. 3 sect. 3 disquisit. magic., Cardan lib. 16 cap. 90 reckons up many magnetical medicines, as to piss through a ring, &c., Mizaldus cent. 3. 30, Baptista Porta, Jason Pratensis, Lobelius pag. 87, Matthiolus, &c., prescribe many absurd remedies. Radix mandragorae ebibitae, Annuli ex ungulis asini, Stercus amatae sub cervicali positum, illa nesciente, &c., quum odorem foeditatis sentit, amor solvitur. Noctuae ovum abstemios facit comestum, ex consilio Iarthae Indorum gymnosophistae apud Philostratum lib. 3. Sanguis amasiae ebibitus omnem amoris sensum tollit, Faustinam Marci Aurelii uxorem, gladiatoris amore captam, ita penitus consilio Chaldaeorum liberatam, refert Julius
Capitolinus [A drink of mandrake root, rings of asses’ hoofs, faeces of the beloved placed under the pillow without her knowing, etc., when he smells the foul odour, the love will be dissolved. Eating the egg of a night owl causes abstinence, in the opinion of Iarchas the Indian gymnosophist in Philostratus, Bk 3. Drinking the blood of mistresses removes all feeling of love. Faustina, the wife of Marcus Aurelius, captivated by love for a gladiator, was completely freed in this way by the advice of the Chaldeans, according to Julius Capitolinus]. Some of our Astrologers will effect as much by Characteristical Images, ex Sigillis Hermetis, Salomonis, Chaelis, &c., mulieris imago habentis crines sparsos, &c. [from seals of Hermes, Solomon, Chael, etc., the image of a woman with her hair spread out, etc.] Our old Poets and Fantastical writers have many fabulous remedies for such as are lovesick, as that of Protesilaus’ tomb in Philostratus, in his dialogue betwixt Phoenix and Vinitor: Vinitor upon occasion discoursing of the rare virtues of that shrine, telleth him that Protesilaus’ Altar and Tomb cures almost all manner of diseases, consumptions, dropsies, quartan agues, sore eyes: and amongst the rest, such as are lovesick, shall there be helped. But the most famous is The moral is, vehement Fear expels Love.Leucata Petra, that renowned Rock in Greece, of which Strabo writes, Geog. lib. 10, not far from Saint Maura’s, saith Sandys lib. 1. From which rock if any Lover flung himself down headlong, he was instantly cured. Venus after the death of Adonis when she could take no rest for love,

l.hi: Cum vesana suas torreret flamma medullas,

lg.l: [When a raging fire burned her to the core,]

div.p: came to the Temple of Apollo to know what she should do to be eased of her pain: Apollo sent her to Leucata Petra, where she precipitated herself, and was forthwith freed, and when she would needs know of him a reason of it, he told her again, that he had often observed Jupiter when he was enamoured on Juno, thither go to ease and wash himself, and after him diverse others. Cephalus for the love of Protela, Degonetus’ daughter, leapt down here, that Lesbian Sappho for Phaon, on whom she miserably doted.

l.hi: Cupidinis oestro percita e summo praeceps ruit,

lg.l: [Inflamed with frenzied desire, she threw herself headlong off the summit,]

div.p: hoping thus to ease herself, and to be freed of her love pangs.

l.hi: Hic se Deucalion Pyrrhae succensus amore

lg.l: Hither Deucalion came, when Pyrrha’s love
Tormented him, and leapt down to the sea,
And had no harm at all, but by and by
His love was gone and chased quite away.

div.p: This medicine Jos. Scaliger speaks of, Ausoniarum lectionum lib. 18, Salmuth in Pancirol. de 7 mundi mirac. and other writers. Pliny reports that amongst the Cyzeni, there is a Well consecrated to Cupid, of which if any lover taste, his passion is mitigated: and Anthony Verderius Imag. deorum, de Cupid. saith, that amongst the Ancients there was Amor Lethes, he took burning torches, and extinguished them in the river; his statua was to be seen in the Temple of Venus Elusina, of which Ovid makes mention, and saith, that all lovers of old went thither on pilgrimage, that would be rid of their love pangs. Pausanias in Lib. 10.Phocicis, writes of a Temple dedicated, Veneri in spelunca, to Venus in the vault, at Naupactus in Achaia (now Lepanto), in which your widows that would have second husbands, made their supplications to the Goddess; all manner of suits concerning Lovers were commenced, and their grievances helped. The same Author in Achaicis, tells as much of the river Rhodiginus ant. lect. lib. 16 cap. 25 calls it Selenus. Omni amore liberat [It frees from all love].Senelus in Greece; if any Lover washed himself in it, by a secret virtue of that water (by reason of the extreme coldness belike), he was healed of Love’s torments,

l.hi: Amoris vulnus idem qui sanat facit;

lg.l: [The same one that causes the wound of love heals it;]

div.p: which if it be so, that water as he holds, is omni auro pretiosior, better than any gold. Where none of all these remedies will take place, I know no other, but that all Lovers must make an head, and rebel, as they did in Cupido crucifixus, lepidum poema [Cupid Crucified, an elegant poem].Ausonius, and crucify Cupid till he grant their request, or satisfy their desires.
